mainTopic: Two wives' כתובה claims in a circle, the wife's 'I only did it to please my husband' excuse, and whether a creditor may take sold land when the free land is blighted
overview: The amud opens by finishing a story about two deeds dated in ניסן. רב יוסף shows a man why a document to collect only from אייר onward will not work, and the fix is that the two deed holders write each other a הרשאה. Then a new משנה teaches that when a man with two wives sells a field and only the first wife waives her claim to the buyer, the claims go around in a circle until they make a פשרה. The גמרא asks how a bare waiver can work, and answers that she backed it with a קנין. It then asks why she cannot say 'I only did it to please my husband,' as a משנה in גיטין allows. רב חסדא, רב פפא and רב אשי each give a different way to fit the two משניות together. A new question follows: if the debtor's free land gets blighted, may a creditor take land he already sold? The גמרא tries to prove the answer from רבי מאיר's ruling and from רבא's ברייתא about 'I left you a place to collect from.' It rejects the proof, because there the person lost his rights by his own action. The amud ends as רב יימר begins to speak to רב אשי, and his words come on the next amud.

steps.title: רב יוסף turns down a request to collect only from אייר onward
steps.stepSummary: A man asked רב יוסף to write him a טירפא allowing him to collect from buyers from אייר onward. רב יוסף explained that the buyers could push back against him.
steps.simpleTranslation: [The man asked: write for me] a document of repossession from אייר and on. רב יוסף said to him: The buyers can say to you, 'You are from the first of ניסן!'
steps.whatsHappening: The text opens at the end of a man's request from the previous discussion. רב יוסף rejects the request by showing the argument the buyers would use against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's deed just says 'ניסן', so it could be from the very first day of the month. That would make it earlier than the other deed, which is dated the fifth of ניסן. In that case, the buyers can say the field he already holds is rightfully his, and that he should go after the other man instead of taking their land.

keyTerms.meaning: A court document that lets a creditor take back property that the debtor sold
The month after ניסן
They can say to you
From (dated) the first of ניסן

phrases.english: a document of repossession from Iyyar and on.
He said to him: They can say to you:
phrases.notes: 'They' are the buyers he wants to collect from.

phrases.english: You are from the first of Nisan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: יָכְלִי לְמֵימַר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the two deeds from ניסן from the previous section
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the man's request for a טירפא dated from אייר onward
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: His undated ניסן deed could be the earlier one, so buyers can send him back to the other deed holder

steps.title: So how can this man fix his problem?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what this man can do, since he seems stuck.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is his remedy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how this man can protect himself. It is setting up the practical solution that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each deed holder can be pushed off by the buyers in his own way. So the question is how they can still collect what they are owed.

keyTerms.meaning: What is his fix / remedy?

phrases.english: What is his remedy?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי תַּקַּנְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from רב יוסף's rejection
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical way for the deed holder to collect despite the buyers' argument

steps.title: The fix: they write each other a power of attorney
steps.stepSummary: The two deed holders give each other a הרשאה, so either one can collect on behalf of the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them write a power of attorney to each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the solution: each deed holder writes the other a הרשאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once each man can also collect in the other's name, the buyers can no longer say 'go after the other one.' Whichever deed turns out to be first, the collector holds both rights.

keyTerms.meaning: A document giving someone power to act or collect for you
To each other

steps.whatToRemember: When two creditors could each be pushed off onto the other, writing a הרשאה to each other closes the gap.

phrases.english: Let them write a power of attorney to each other.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִכְתְּבוּ הַרְשָׁאָה לַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Mutual הרשאה lets either party collect regardless of which deed is earlier

steps.title: Two wives, a sold field, and an endless circle
steps.stepSummary: A man with two wives sells a field. Only the first wife tells the buyer she has no claim on him. Each party can take the field from the next in a circle, so they must reach a פשרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man was married to two wives and sold his field. The first wife wrote to the buyer, 'I have no legal claim against you.' The second wife takes the field from the buyer. The first wife takes it from the second. The buyer takes it from the first. They go around in a circle until they make a compromise between them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It describes a case where three claims block each other in a loop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second wife never gave up her claim, so her כתובה lien lets her take the field from the buyer. The first wife's כתובה is earlier, so she outranks the second wife. But the first wife gave up her rights to the buyer, so he can take the field back from her. No one can win for good, so they must make a פשרה.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה
I have no legal claim or dealings with you
Buyer
She takes it away (collects)
They go around in a circle
Compromise

steps.confusionAlert: Each 'taking' is fully legal on its own. The circle is not a punishment; it simply has no natural end.

phrases.english: Mishnah
One who was married to two wives
and sold his field,
and the first wife wrote to the buyer
'I have no legal claim or dealings with you' —
the second takes it from the buyer,
and the first from the second,
and the buyer from the first.
And they go around in a circle,
until they make a compromise between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי שֶׁהָיָה נָשׂוּי שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים וּמָכַר אֶת שָׂדֵהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New משנה; a new topic begins
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the first wife waives her claim only to the buyer, the claims form a circle that ends only with a פשרה

steps.title: The same rule for creditors
steps.stepSummary: The משנה applies the same circle to two creditors, and to a woman creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so too with a creditor, and so too with a woman creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה extends its rule beyond wives to creditors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picture two creditors where the earlier one gave up his claim only to the buyer. The same loop forms. Mentioning a woman creditor shows that the rule is about the order of liens, not about כתובה specifically.

keyTerms.meaning: Creditor
A woman who is a creditor

steps.whatToRemember: An earlier lien beats a later one, but a waiver given to one person only can create a loop with no winner.

phrases.english: And so too a creditor,
and so too a woman creditor.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן בַּעַל חוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the משנה's ruling to other cases
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The circular result applies equally to creditors

steps.title: Does saying 'I have no dealings' even count?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה with a ברייתא. That ברייתא says that statements like 'I have no claim on this field' mean nothing legally.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if she wrote this to him, what of it? Isn't it taught: One who says to his fellow, 'I have no legal claim on this field,' or 'I have no business with it,' or 'My hands are removed from it,' has said nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the first wife's words should have any legal effect. It brings a ברייתא that says such words are empty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole circle in the משנה depends on the first wife's waiver working against the buyer. But the ברייתא teaches that a bare statement giving up rights to a field does nothing. So how can the buyer use her words to take the field back from her?

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
What of it? What difference does it make?
But isn't it taught (in a ברייתא)?
My hands are removed from it
He has said nothing (it has no legal effect)

phrases.english: Gemara
And if she wrote to him, what of it?
But isn't it taught: One who says to his fellow

phrases.aramaic: ״דִּין וּדְבָרִים אֵין לִי עַל שָׂדֶה זוֹ״,
phrases.english: 'I have no legal claim on this field,'
or 'I have no business with it,'
or 'My hands are removed from it' —
has said nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי כָּתְבָה לֵיהּ מַאי הָוֵי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption behind the משנה
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's assumption that the first wife's written waiver is binding
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules that a bare declaration giving up rights to a field has no legal force

steps.title: Answer: she backed her words with a קנין
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a case where the buyer made a formal קנין with the first wife, so her waiver is binding.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where they made a קנין from her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that in the משנה, the waiver was sealed with a formal act of קנין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words alone, as in the ברייתא, do nothing. A waiver confirmed by a קנין is legally binding. So the משנה and the ברייתא do not clash; they are talking about different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
They made a formal act of acquisition (קנין) with her

steps.whatToRemember: A bare 'I have no claim' means nothing; with a קנין it becomes a binding waiver.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where they made an act of acquisition from her.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first wife's waiver was only words, which the ברייתא says are meaningless
steps.terutzMaskana: The waiver was confirmed with a קנין, so it is binding

steps.title: Even with a formal acquisition, she can say she only wanted to please her husband
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 7. A קנין from the wife should not help, because she can claim she only went along to keep peace with her husband. A משנה in גיטין seems to prove this.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if they made a קנין with her, so what? Let her say: 'I only did it to please my husband.' Didn't we learn in a משנה: if someone bought from the husband and then went back and bought from the wife, his purchase is void? So we see that she can say, 'I only did it to please my husband.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is attacking the answer it just gave. It argues that a formal קנין with the wife still should not bind her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 said the first wife's waiver works because the buyer made a קנין with her. The גמרא now says a קנין does not settle it, because she can claim she was not serious and only wanted to avoid fighting with her husband. A משנה in גיטין rules exactly this way: a later purchase from the wife does not hold.

keyTerms.meaning: They made a formal act of acquisition (קנין) with her
Pleasing someone, keeping someone happy
Didn't we learn in a משנה? (introduces a source used as a challenge)
His purchase is void
Apparently, so we see

steps.confusionAlert: The wife's excuse is not that the קנין was technically flawed. She admits she did it. Her claim is that she did not really mean it, because she only went along to avoid a fight with her husband.

phrases.english: And if they made a formal acquisition with her, what of it?
Let her say: I did it only to please my husband.
Didn't we learn in a משנה:
If someone bought property from the man
and then went back and bought her rights from the wife
his purchase is void.
So we see: she is able to say
I did it only to please my husband.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי קָנוּ מִיָּדָהּ מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 7 that a קנין makes the wife's waiver binding.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 7 that a קנין with the first wife makes her waiver binding.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in גיטין voids a purchase made from the wife after the husband sold. This shows she can always claim 'I only did it to please my husband,' so even a קנין should not bind her.

steps.title: The two משניות follow different תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא, quoting רב חסדא, answers that there is no contradiction. Our משנה follows רבי מאיר and the משנה in גיטין follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said in the name of רב חסדא: It is not difficult. This משנה follows רבי מאיר, and that משנה follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the two sources simply follow two different opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not try to make the two משניות agree. It accepts that they rule differently. According to רבי מאיר, the wife cannot back out with the 'please my husband' excuse, which fits our משנה. According to רבי יהודה, she can, which fits the משנה in גיטין.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction
This one... that one... (matching each source to a different opinion)
A תנא; here, he holds that the wife's agreement binds her
A תנא; here, he holds that the wife can say she only did it to please her husband

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא,
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said that Rav Chisda said:
It is not difficult:
This one is Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is our משנה, with the two wives and the circle of claims.

phrases.english: and that one is Rabbi Yehuda.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the משנה in גיטין that was just quoted.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: הָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר, הָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from step 8 by assigning each משנה to a different תנא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Dispute of תנאים: each source follows a different opinion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think both משניות share one rule, so they would contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה follows רבי מאיר, who holds the wife's agreement binds her. The משנה in גיטין follows רבי יהודה, who lets her say she only did it to please her husband.

steps.title: The ברייתא where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to show that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה really do argue about whether a wife can say 'I only did it to please my husband.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: If a husband wrote a sale document to a first buyer and his wife did not sign it, and then wrote one to a second buyer and she did sign it, she has lost her כתובה. These are the words of רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: She can say, 'I only did it to please my husband. You, what claim do you have against me?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source that proves the argument it just mentioned. רבי מאיר says her signature costs her the כתובה, and רבי יהודה says she can back out with the 'please my husband' excuse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wife's choice not to sign for the first buyer shows she knew how to refuse. So רבי מאיר treats her signature for the second buyer as a real giving up of her rights. רבי יהודה says even that signature can be explained away as keeping the peace at home, so it does not bind her.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
She signed (agreeing to the sale)
She has lost her כתובה (her right to collect it)
You, what claim do you have against me?

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר holds that a wife who agrees to her husband's sale is bound by it. That is why our משנה works when the buyer made a קנין with her. רבי יהודה holds she can always say 'I only did it to please my husband,' which is the view of the משנה in גיטין.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties our משנה's circle of claims to one side of a dispute between תנאים. The case only works according to רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא:
If he wrote a sale document to the first buyer
and she did not sign it for him,
and then wrote one to the second buyer, and she signed it for him,
she has lost her כתובה,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
She is able to say:
"I did it only to please my husband;
you, what claim do you have against me?"

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: כָּתַב לָרִאשׁוֹן וְלֹא חָתְמָה לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the dispute between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה that step 9 relied on.
steps.raayaObject: The claim in step 9 that רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue about whether a wife can say 'I only did it to please my husband.'
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a wife who refused to sign for the first buyer but signed for the second.

steps.title: Would רבי really split the anonymous משניות between two opinions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא's answer. It is hard to believe רבי wrote our anonymous משנה like רבי מאיר and the anonymous משנה in גיטין like רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Would רבי write the anonymous משנה here like רבי מאיר, and the anonymous משנה there like רבי יהודה?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 9, which said each משנה follows a different תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When רבי writes a משנה without a name (סתם), he is showing which opinion he holds as the main one. It would be strange for him to pick רבי מאיר in one place and רבי יהודה in another on the same question. So the 'two תנאים' answer looks weak.

keyTerms.meaning: An anonymous משנה with no name attached, usually showing the accepted view
רבי יהודה הנשיא, who arranged the משנה
Here / there

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבִּי, סָתֵם לַהּ הָכָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
phrases.english: And would Rabbi write it anonymously here like Rabbi Meir
phrases.notes: 'רבי' here means רבי יהודה הנשיא, the one who put the משנה together.

phrases.english: and write it anonymously there like Rabbi Yehuda?!
phrases.notes: 'There' is the משנה in גיטין from step 8.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי, סָתֵם לַהּ הָכָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְסָתֵם לַהּ הָתָם כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the 'two תנאים' answer of רב חסדא that step 10 had supported
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's answer that our משנה follows רבי מאיר and the משנה in גיטין follows רבי יהודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי would not likely write two anonymous משניות that follow opposite opinions on the same issue.

steps.title: רב פפא: the משנה is about a divorced woman
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says our משנה is about a woman who wrote the waiver after she was divorced. Everyone agrees her waiver counts, so there is no conflict.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: our משנה is about a divorced woman, and everyone agrees with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a new answer. Both משניות can follow everyone's view, because our משנה is talking about a divorcée.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The excuse 'I only did it to please my husband' works only while she is married. A divorced woman has no husband to please, so her waiver is binding according to everyone. The משנה in גיטין, where she can use the excuse, is about a married woman.

keyTerms.meaning: A divorced woman
Everyone agrees

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is about a divorced woman, and it is the opinion of everyone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בִּגְרוּשָׁה, וְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11 by changing the case of our משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה is about a married woman and seems to follow רבי מאיר against the משנה in גיטין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה is about a divorcée, so everyone agrees her waiver counts and there is no dispute at all.

steps.title: רב אשי: everything follows רבי מאיר, who only applies his rule with two buyers
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says both משניות follow רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר says the wife cannot claim 'I did it to please my husband' only when there were two buyers. Our משנה is a two-buyer case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: it all follows רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר said his ruling there only when there were two buyers. The buyers can tell her: 'If you really did it to please your husband, you should have done it for the first buyer too.' But with only one buyer, even רבי מאיר agrees she can use the excuse. Our משנה is a case where the husband had already sold to someone else before.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives another answer. He explains that רבי מאיר's ruling is limited, so the משנה in גיטין (one buyer) and our משנה (two buyers) can both follow him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two buyers, the wife refused to sign for the first one and signed for the second. That shows she was not just pleasing her husband, because then she would have signed both times. With one buyer there is no such proof, so even רבי מאיר lets her say 'I did it to please him.' Our משנה is a case where an earlier sale happened without her signing.

keyTerms.meaning: Two buyers
Keeping someone happy; here, pleasing the husband
One buyer
Agrees

steps.whatToRemember: There are three answers to the contradiction. רב חסדא: two different תנאים. רב פפא: our משנה is about a divorcée. רב אשי: all follows רבי מאיר, whose rule applies only when there were two buyers.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read רב אשי's 'even רבי מאיר agrees' as saying the waiver works. It means the opposite: with one buyer, even רבי מאיר agrees she CAN say 'I did it to please my husband.'

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is all the view of Rabbi Meir,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר הָתָם,
phrases.english: and Rabbi Meir only said his view there
phrases.notes: 'There' means the ברייתא from step 10 where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue.

phrases.english: in a case of two buyers,
because they can say to her:
If it is true that you did it to please your husband,
you should have done it for the first buyer.
But with one buyer,
even Rabbi Meir agrees.
phrases.notes: He agrees that she can say she only did it to please her husband.

phrases.english: And our Mishna is where he had written a sale to another buyer.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the קשיא of step 11 instead of רב פפא's
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a תנא's ruling, plus narrowing the case of our משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר never lets a wife say 'I did it to please my husband,' so the משנה in גיטין cannot follow him.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר blocks the excuse only with two buyers. The משנה in גיטין is a one-buyer case and our משנה is a two-buyer case, so both follow רבי מאיר.

steps.title: New topic: a creditor collects from unsold land first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה in גיטין. A creditor may not collect from land the debtor already sold if the debtor still has unsold land, even very poor land.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: a creditor does not collect from sold (liened) property when there is free, unsold property, even if the free property is the worst-quality land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new section by quoting a rule from a משנה in גיטין. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land the debtor sold is still tied up by the debt (משועבדים), but the buyers are protected as long as the debtor has his own land left. The creditor must take from the debtor's free land first, even if it is זיבורית, the worst grade.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned in a משנה elsewhere
Property tied up by a debt that was sold to someone else
Free property still owned by the debtor
The worst-quality land

phrases.english: We learned there:
One does not collect from property that was sold but is tied up by the debt
where there is free, unsold property,
even if it is the worst-quality land.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן הָתָם: אֵין נִפְרָעִין מִנְּכָסִים מְשׁוּעְבָּדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the wife's waiver ends
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A creditor must collect from the debtor's free land, even the worst grade, before taking sold land from buyers.

steps.title: What if the free land gets ruined?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the debtor's free land is blighted and no longer worth enough, may the creditor take the sold land?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the free land became blighted, what is the law? May the creditor take from the sold property?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question that builds on the משנה it just quoted. The next steps try to answer it from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the free land must be used first. Here the free land existed but was later ruined. The question is whether the buyers' protection disappears once the free land is ruined, or whether they stay protected.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked before the חכמים
Became blighted or ruined
To seize property from a buyer to pay a debt

phrases.english: A question was asked before them:
If the free property became blighted,
what is the law, may he seize from the sold property?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: אִישְׁתְּדוּף בְּנֵי חָרֵי, מַהוּ דְּלִיטְרוֹף מִמְּשַׁעְבְּדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a case the משנה in step 14 did not cover
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a creditor may collect from sold property once the debtor's free property has been ruined.

steps.title: Quoting רבי מאיר's ruling about a wife who signed for only the second buyer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to try to answer the question about blighted land. A husband sold to two buyers, and his wife signed only for the second. רבי מאיר says she lost her כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A husband wrote a bill of sale to a first buyer and his wife did not sign it. Then he sold to a second buyer and she did sign. רבי מאיר says she has lost her כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is bringing a source to try to answer the question from Step 15. This step only quotes the case; the next step explains how it proves something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wife signed for the second buyer, which means she gave up her claim on that field. She never signed for the first buyer. Even so, רבי מאיר rules that she lost her כתובה, and the גמרא will use that ruling as its proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: the גמרא is bringing a source to answer a question
She signed, meaning the wife signed to give up her claim on that field
She lost her כתובה, the money owed to her by her כתובה

phrases.english: Come and hear:
He wrote [a bill of sale] to the first [buyer]
phrases.notes: 'He' is the husband, who is selling his fields.

phrases.english: and she did not sign for him,
[then he sold] to the second, and she signed for him
she has lost her כתובה,
these are the words of רבי מאיר.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to try to answer the question of Step 15.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether a creditor may take sold land when the debtor's free land became blighted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with רבי מאיר's ruling about a wife who signed only for the second buyer.

steps.title: The proof: she should at least collect from the first buyer
steps.stepSummary: If blighted free land let a creditor go back to sold land, the wife should still collect from the first buyer. Since רבי מאיר says she lost everything, it seems the creditor cannot go back to sold land.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you think that when the free land is blighted the creditor can take sold land, then even though she lost her rights against the second buyer, she should at least collect from the first buyer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ruling in Step 16 answers the question. רבי מאיר's ruling only makes sense if blighted free land does not let a creditor take sold land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the first field was sold, the husband still owned the second field, so the first buyer left her land to collect from. She later gave that land up by signing, so it became unreachable for her, just like blighted land. If unreachable free land let her go back to the first buyer, she would collect from him. Since רבי מאיר says she lost her כתובה, the answer must be no.

keyTerms.meaning: If it should enter your mind, meaning if you were to think
Became blighted or ruined
Free land, meaning land the debtor still owns and has not sold
Liened land, meaning land the debtor already sold that still carries the debt
Takes away or seizes the land for the debt

steps.confusionAlert: Nothing in this case was really blighted. The second field is 'lost' to her only because she signed it away. The גמרא treats that like blighted land.

phrases.english: And if it should enter your mind
[that if] the free land became blighted
he may seize from the liened [sold] land,
granted that she lost her כתובה from the second [buyer],
she should at least collect from the first!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אִישְׁתְּדוּף בְּנֵי חָרֵי טָרֵיף מִמְּשַׁעְבְּדִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the ברייתא quoted in Step 16 answers the question.
steps.raayaObject: That a creditor may not take sold land even when the free land became blighted.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי מאיר's ruling that she lost her כתובה completely, even though she never signed for the first buyer.

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק: she lost only her rights against the second buyer
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק reads 'she lost' as lost only against the second buyer. Then the ברייתא proves nothing about blighted land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: What does 'she lost' mean? She lost her rights against the second buyer.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק pushes back on the proof. He says the ברייתא never said she cannot collect from the first buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on reading 'lost' as lost from everyone. If it only means lost from the second buyer, she may still collect from the first. Then the ברייתא may even fit the view that blighted free land lets a creditor take sold land.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who reads 'lost' narrowly
What does it mean?

phrases.english: רב נחמן בר יצחק said:
What does 'she lost' mean?
She lost [her rights] from the second [buyer].

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מַאי ״אִיבְּדָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 17 by reading the ברייתא differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof drawn from רבי מאיר's ruling.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed 'she lost' means lost completely, but it could mean lost only from the second buyer.

steps.title: רבא's first answer: 'lost' means lost completely
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he has two answers against רב נחמן בר יצחק. The first is that the word 'lost' means lost completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: There are two answers to this. One: 'she lost' means she lost entirely.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן בר יצחק's reading and says he has two answers. In this step he gives the first one, which is about the plain meaning of the word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain sense of 'she lost her כתובה' is that she lost all of it, not just one buyer's part. So the narrow reading goes against the simple wording, and the original proof stands.

keyTerms.meaning: There are two answers to this, meaning two ways to reject a statement
Completely, entirely
It means, or this is how it sounds

phrases.english: רבא said:
There are two answers to this matter,
one: that 'she lost' means entirely.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: שְׁתֵּי תְּשׁוּבוֹת בַּדָּבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן בר יצחק's narrow reading in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר יצחק's reading that 'she lost' means only from the second buyer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plain meaning of 'she lost' is a total loss, so the narrow reading does not fit the words.

steps.title: רבא's second answer: a ברייתא about a creditor who waived his claim against the second buyer
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if a creditor gives up his claim against the second buyer, he cannot collect from the first buyer either. The first buyer left him land to collect from.
steps.simpleTranslation: Also, a ברייתא teaches: A man borrowed from one person and sold his land to two buyers. The creditor wrote to the second buyer, 'I have no claim against you.' Then he has no claim at all against the first buyer, because the first buyer can say, 'I left you a place to collect from.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his second answer. He brings a ברייתא that clearly says a creditor in this kind of case cannot collect from the first buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is exactly like the wife's case. The creditor himself gave up the second buyer's land, so the first buyer can say he left enough land to cover the debt. This supports reading 'she lost' as lost completely, and it brings back the original proof that land which became unreachable does not let a creditor take sold land.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
I have no legal claim against you, a formula for giving up a claim
Buyer
I left you a place to collect from

steps.whatToRemember: A buyer can tell the creditor, 'When I bought, I left you land to collect from.' If that land later becomes unreachable, here because the creditor himself gave it up, the creditor still cannot come to this buyer. This is why רבי מאיר says the wife lost her כתובה completely.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'I left you a place to collect from' protects earlier buyers. The גמרא tries to use it to answer the question of Step 15, but the next step rejects that proof, because here the creditor gave up the land himself.

phrases.english: And furthermore, it was taught [in a ברייתא]:
[If] he borrowed from one [person]
and sold his property to two [buyers],
and the creditor wrote to the second buyer:
'I have no legal claim or dealings with you,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לוֹ עַל לוֹקֵחַ רִאשׁוֹן כְּלוּם.
phrases.english: he has nothing against the first buyer.
Because he can say:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the first buyer, speaking to the creditor.

phrases.english: 'I left you a place to collect from.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד, תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא's second answer against Step 18, backing up the first answer with an explicit ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That 'she lost' means lost completely, and that land which became unreachable does not let a creditor take sold land.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא where a creditor gave up his claim against the second buyer and so cannot collect from the first buyer.

steps.title: There he lost out by his own action
steps.stepSummary: The proof from the ברייתא is rejected. In that case the person caused his own loss by signing away his rights, which is not the same as land being ruined by nature.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is he himself who caused his own loss with his own hands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the attempt to learn the law of blighted land from the ברייתא about giving up a claim against the second buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the creditor (or wife) wrote 'I have no claim against you' to the second buyer, so the loss came from his own action. That is why he cannot go back to the first buyer. When land becomes blighted, nobody chose to lose anything, so the creditor may still be allowed to go back to sold land. The question about blighted land stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: There, in that other case (the ברייתא)
He caused a loss to himself
With his own hands, by his own direct action

steps.whyThisMatters: This creates a key difference between losing your rights by your own choice and losing them because of something outside your control, like the land being ruined.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not decide that a creditor CAN go back to sold land after the free land is blighted. It only shows that the ברייתא does not prove he CANNOT. The question is still unanswered.

phrases.english: There
phrases.notes: He means the case in the ברייתא, where the creditor wrote to the second buyer that he had no claim against him.

phrases.english: it is he who caused a loss to himself with his own hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם אִיהוּ דְּאַפְסֵיד נַפְשֵׁיהּ בְּיָדַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects using the ברייתא from step 20 as proof about blighted land.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the comparison to blighted land. The ruling of the ברייתא itself stays in place.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא is about a loss the person caused himself on purpose. Blighted land is a loss that came from outside, so the two cases are different.

steps.title: רב יימר begins speaking to רב אשי
steps.stepSummary: An opening line. רב יימר is about to say something to רב אשי, and his words come in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא tells us that רב יימר is about to speak to רב אשי, and what he says comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is ruled here yet. The line only tells us who is speaking and to whom, so the learner should get ready for a new question or point in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who discusses questions with רב אשי
A leading אמורא, one of the people who put the תלמוד together

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Ashi:

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the next move after the proof from the ברייתא was rejected.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line only tells us who is speaking, and his statement follows.
